title: Trimming rabbit nails
subtitle: Overgrown nails catch on bedding and curl into the foot pad. Six weeks between trims keeps them right.
excerpt: Rabbit nails grow continuously and curl inward if left uncut. A nail that has curled into the pad requires a vet visit; a nail at the right stage takes thirty seconds per foot with a pair of small animal clippers. Here is how to identify the quick, choose the cutting angle, and handle the few that bleed.
sourceNotes: British Rabbit Council welfare notes on nail care. RSPCA rabbit husbandry guide. Judith Bell, Rabbits (Crowood Animal Series, 2012), grooming chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: The blood vessel and nerve running through the centre of the nail. Cutting into the quick causes pain and bleeding. On pale nails it is visible as a pink line; on dark nails it requires estimation from the nail base.

content.text: Rabbit nails grow in a gentle curve. The right time to cut is when that curve is obvious but before the nail starts to turn back toward the pad. For most breeds that is every six weeks; larger breeds like Flemish Giants may need trimming every four. Cut into
and you will have a rabbit that does not forgive nail days for a while.

Two approaches. The first is the lap position: sit with the rabbit's back against your stomach, its legs pointing outward and its head resting between your arm and body. This lets you reach all four feet without assistance but requires the rabbit to be relaxed.
The second is a two-person approach: one person holds the rabbit wrapped loosely in a towel, the other trims. Expose one foot at a time through the towel. This is better for an uncooperative animal.
Hold the foot firmly and extend one nail at a time by pressing gently below the toe joint.
For pale or white nails: hold the nail up to a torch or bright window. The pink quick is visible inside. Cut 3-4 mm below where the pink ends.
For dark nails: estimate from the nail base. The quick extends roughly two-thirds of the way along the nail. Cut the outermost third, at an angle matching the nail tip, not straight across.
Cut quickly and decisively. A slow squeeze with blunt clippers crushes the nail before cutting; a sharp, fast cut is cleaner and less uncomfortable.

Press a pinch of styptic powder against the bleeding tip for fifteen seconds. If you have no styptic powder, cornflour works as an alternative. The bleeding stops within two minutes in almost all cases. Clipping the quick is painful; put the rabbit down and let it settle before continuing.

Mark the trim date in the hutch log or on a calendar. Consistency matters more than the exact interval. Rabbits kept on wire flooring wear nails down faster than those on solid flooring with soft bedding; adjust the frequency based on what you see rather than the calendar alone.

Nails that have grown so long they curve back into the pad need a vet visit. Attempting to cut a nail that is pressing on the pad without examining and possibly lancing the wound underneath it risks introducing infection.
